subject: philosophy
title: Validity and soundness
objective: Test the inference without confusing it with the truth of its premises.

lesson.opening: The next distinction applies to deductive arguments. In ordinary language, valid may mean acceptable. Here it has a precise technical meaning concerning possible combinations of truth and falsity.

sections.heading: A valid structure is not enough
sections.body:
A deductive argument is valid when there is no possible case in which all its premises are true and its conclusion false. To test validity, temporarily grant the premises—even strange ones—and ask whether the conclusion must then follow. You are examining a relationship, not endorsing a worldview.

All whales are birds. All birds have wings. Therefore all whales have wings. The argument has a valid form, although a premise is false. Soundness requires both validity and true premises. This example is not sound. By contrast, a conclusion that happens to be true does not rescue an invalid inference used to reach it.

Consider “If the alarm is active, the light is on; the light is on; so the alarm is active.” The light might be on for a maintenance test. The inference affirms the consequent: if P then Q; Q; therefore P. Compare the valid form modus ponens: if P then Q; P; therefore Q.

The truth of premises and the validity of inference need different kinds of work. Evidence about how a device functions may establish a premise. A countermodel—a possible assignment with true premises and a false conclusion—can refute the proposed deductive entailment. Once you have one, more favorable examples do not repair that form.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: Let P mean membership in A and Q mean being insured. The proposed inference is P → Q, Q, therefore P. Setting P false and Q true makes both premises true but the conclusion false. That is enough to show invalidity.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: The author might add “Only collection A manuscripts are insured.” That would change the argument by adding Q → P. A successful repair must acknowledge the new premise and provide grounds for it.

activities.prompt: Why does the manuscript conclusion fail to follow?
choices: Insurance might also cover manuscripts outside collection A.

activities.prompt: Arrange a valid modus ponens inference.
items: If the seal is intact, the container is unopened.

activities.prompt: All cats are reptiles. All reptiles are cold-blooded. Therefore all cats are cold-blooded. This is…
choices: Invalid because the conclusion is false.

activities.prompt: Which added premise repairs the manuscript inference?
choices: Only collection A manuscripts are insured.

activities.prompt: Which follows from an argument’s soundness?
choices: Its premises may all be false.

activities.prompt: Construct an invalid argument with a true conclusion. Explain why the conclusion’s truth does not make the inference valid.
activities.context: If a manuscript is in collection A, then it is insured. This manuscript is insured. Therefore it is in collection A.
rubric: I show a possible case where premises hold but the conclusion fails, using the same structure.
I distinguish actual truth from entailment.
